recall_prompt: Say how you would count the positive divisors of 1080 — the prime factorisation, and how the count comes from the exponents.
insider_note: The first mark is the factorisation written in full: 1080 = 2³ · 3³ · 5. Then each exponent gains 1 before multiplying — (3 + 1)(3 + 1)(1 + 1) = 32 — and the +1 on the single 5 is the one most often dropped.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Prime factorisation of 1080

recall.must_convey: That 1080 is factorised into primes as 2 cubed times 3 cubed times 5.
accept: one thousand eighty is two cubed into three cubed into five
prime factorise, two to the three, three to the three, five to the one
one zero eight zero is eight into twenty seven into five
ten eighty ni primes ga rasthe two cube three cube five
break it into prime powers first

steps.why: Every positive divisor of 1080 is 2ᵃ·3ᵇ·5ᶜ with a, b, c chosen from the exponents available, so the count can only be read off once the prime factorisation is written.
common_mistakes: Writing 1080 = 2² · 3³ · 10 and leaving a non-prime factor.
Miscounting the power of 2: 1080/8 = 135, so 2³ is right and 2⁴ is not.

steps.label: Multiply (exponent + 1) for each prime

recall.must_convey: That the number of divisors is the product of each exponent plus one, 4 times 4 times 2 = 32.
accept: add one to each exponent and multiply, four into four into two is thirty two
three plus one times three plus one times one plus one is thirty two
exponents ki one add chesi multiply, thirty two

steps.why: The exponent of 2 in a divisor can be 0, 1, 2 or 3 — four choices — and likewise for 3 and 5; the choices are independent, so they multiply. The count 32 includes 1 and 1080 itself.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the +1 on the prime 5, giving 16.
